title: Inter Discipline Check: 5 Essential Disciplines Covered
text:
Instrumentation

 Inter Discipline Check: 5 Disciplines Engineers Coordinate

 A P&ID that looks perfect on paper can still send a project back for rework.

 This review step catches that before a single cable is pulled or a single nozzle is welded.

 
 Inter Discipline Check 
 IDC 
 P&ID Review 
 EPC Engineering 
 




 Inter Discipline Check makes sure design output from one engineering department actually works for every other department that has to build around it.


 
 Hello everyone, today we are going to learn Inter Discipline Check, the review step that lines up process, mechanical, piping, civil and electrical design before construction begins.


 We will cover what each discipline checks, the documents involved, who performs the review, and why skipping it gets expensive fast.


 
 
 
 What Is Inter Discipline Check


 Inter Discipline Check, usually shortened to IDC, is a formal review step where every engineering discipline on a project checks its own design output against the documents produced by every other discipline.


 The goal is simple. A P&ID drawn by the process team, a layout drawn by the piping team, and a cable schedule drawn by the electrical team all have to describe the same physical plant. IDC is where a design engineer confirms they actually do.


 This review happens before drawings are issued for construction, since a conflict caught on paper costs far less than the same conflict caught on site with a crane already in place.


 
 Did You Know

 IDC is sometimes called a squad check in EPC contracts. Both names describe the same review, engineers from every discipline sitting together and checking one drawing set against another before it gets issued.




 
 
 Advertisement 


 
 


 5 Disciplines an Inter Discipline Check Covers


 A real IDC touches every discipline that has to physically build around the same equipment, so each one reviews a different slice of the same design.


 
 
 1

 Process and Chemical

 Reviews the P&ID itself, instrument legend, process connection sizes, signal types, and which instruments belong to a vendor package versus the main plant.

 

 
 2

 Mechanical

 Reviews vendor package specifications, PLC and HMI preferences, control panel enclosure material, and the cabling inside a skid.

 

 
 3

 Piping

 Reviews the 3D model for instrument connection details, cable tray routing on pipe racks, and alignment with hookup drawings.

 

 
 4

 Civil and Structural

 Reviews layout drawings for wall and floor cutouts, since cable routes have to physically pass through a structure that civil already designed.

 

 
 5

 Electrical

 Reviews the load list against the P&ID for motor quantity, signal considerations for I/O lists, cable tray layout, and earth pit placement.

 




 
 Tip

 Bring the actual P&ID into the review room, not a summary of it. Most IDC conflicts get caught only when someone traces a real line number across two different discipline drawings side by side.




 
 
 Advertisement 


 
 


 What Instrumentation Checks During an IDC Review


 Since instrumentation sits at the center of most of these documents, an instrument engineer's IDC checklist is usually the longest of the five.


 
 1
 P&ID cross reference. Every instrument on the equipment datasheet and GA drawing matches the tag, service, and location shown on the P&ID.


 2
 Nozzle orientation. A radar level transmitter needs a specific nozzle angle and clearance that the vessel GA drawing has to actually provide.


 3
 Support arrangement. A capacitance type switch or a thermowell needs a mounting support that piping or mechanical has to build into the line.


 4
 Junction box placement. Field junction boxes need a location that does not conflict with a pipe rack, walkway, or equipment maintenance space.





 Reviewing Vendor Packages and Skids


 A vendor supplied skid, a compressor package or a boiler package, brings its own instruments, panels and internal wiring, and none of it was designed with the rest of the plant in mind.


 The mechanical and instrumentation teams have to check that the vendor's PLC make, communication protocol, and HMI specification actually match what the rest of the plant standardizes on, not what the vendor's catalog defaults to.


 Multi section skids add another layer, since cabling that crosses between sections has to be checked for continuity, and any special certification, such as IBR for a boiler package, has to be confirmed before the design is frozen.


 The vendor rarely attends every meeting, so the burden falls on the mechanical and instrumentation teams to translate the vendor's drawing set into something that fits the plant's actual standards, rather than assuming the package will simply drop in as delivered.


 Common Interdisciplinary Items Every Review Catches


 A handful of items show up in nearly every IDC regardless of the project, since they sit at the boundary between two disciplines by nature.


 Cable Tray Routing
 Checked by piping, civil, and electrical together for pipe rack, building, and layout conflicts.


 Control Panel Position
 Checked against equipment layout so operators can actually reach it during maintenance.


 Conduit Routing
 Checked against structural cutouts and other buried or overhead services.


 Instrument Air Tubing
 Checked for tubing runs long enough to reach every pneumatic instrument on the P&ID.



 
 
 Advertisement 


 
 


 Who Performs This Review, and When


 Design engineers inside the plant design or EPC contractor's office perform IDC, not a separate quality department. The same people who drew the documents check them against each other.


 The review happens during the design phase, before drawings move to issued for construction status. Running it earlier, even on a partial drawing set, catches conflicts while a redraw still only costs a few hou
